lede: Ask where something is, not how far it has gone. Pick a point on the line, call it zero, and this graph tracks the position from that point, second by second.
can: Draw a displacement-time graph from a written journey.
Read a velocity as the gradient of one section.
Give a velocity with its sign, and a speed as its size.

text: Where something is, second by second

md: A distance-time graph only ever climbs, because distance keeps adding up. A displacement-time graph can come back down, because displacement is measured from a fixed point and a journey home shrinks it. Pick that point, call it zero, and the steepness of each straight section says how fast the object was going, sign and all.

md: The vertical axis is not a running total of ground covered. It is a live position: how far the body is from the chosen point, with a plus or a minus for which side of it. Read a height and you have read where the body was at that moment.

explain: Straight up from 30 s meets the flat section at 30 m. The robot is parked there, 30 m from the pharmacy door.

md:
A straight section climbs by a fixed number of metres in every second, and that number is the velocity. Take the two ends of the section, subtract the displacements for the rise, subtract the times for the run, then divide.

Use the section's own start time, never the clock reading at its end: the robot's last section lasts $60 - 35 = 25$ s, not 60.

prompt: Work out the velocity of the robot during the first 20 seconds, in m/s.
explain: Rise 30 m, run 20 s, so $30 \div 20 = 1.5$ m/s. The robot is moving away from the pharmacy door.

alt: A table matching the shape of each section to the motion: a line sloping up means moving away with positive velocity; a flat line means at rest; a line sloping down means coming back with negative velocity; below the time axis means the other side of the start.

md: Flat means the position is not changing, so the body has stopped somewhere, not necessarily back at the start. A falling section means the displacement is getting smaller, so the body has turned round and is heading back. That is a negative velocity, and the minus sign is the direction.

title: Why a falling line is not a slowing body
md: A straight section, however steep, has one velocity all the way along it. So a line sloping down is not a body slowing down: it is a body going the other way at a steady rate.

prompt: The robot's last section falls from 30 m to $-20$ m. What is it doing?
options: Travelling back past the pharmacy door at a steady velocity
Slowing down and stopping at the pharmacy door
answer: Travelling back past the pharmacy door at a steady velocity
explain: The section is straight, so the velocity is constant; it is negative, so the robot is travelling the other way; it finishes below zero, so it has passed the door and gone 20 m beyond it.

md: **First section:** rise $= 42 - 0 = 42$ m, run $= 12 - 0 = 12$ s, so the velocity is $42 \div 12 = 3.5$ m/s.

prompt: Your graph is drawn but you cannot see how to get the velocity of one stage. What is worth writing first?
options: The coordinates of the two ends of that stage
The total distance for the whole journey
answer: The coordinates of the two ends of that stage
explain: Two coordinate pairs give you the rise and the run at a glance, and that is exactly what the first mark is for.

md:
**Middle section:** the graph is flat from 12 s to 20 s, so the drone hovers for 8 s, 42 m from the entrance.
**Last section:** rise $= -18 - 42 = -60$ m, run $= 35 - 20 = 15$ s, so the velocity is $-60 \div 15 = -4$ m/s.

title: GCSE Mechanics Further - Displacement Time
why: A Northern Ireland teacher working straight off the CCEA Unit 2 specification. Watch how each section is treated on its own before anything is added up.

prompt: A body is at 60 m when $t = 20$ s and at 12 m when $t = 36$ s. What is its velocity, in m/s?
explain: Rise $= 12 - 60 = -48$ m and run $= 36 - 20 = 16$ s, so $-48 \div 16 = -3$ m/s. Dividing by the clock reading of 36 s would have given $-1.33$.

md:
Distance counts every metre covered, whichever way the body was pointing, so it only grows. Displacement is one signed reading at the end.

For distance, take each sloping section, find the size of its change, and add the sizes. For displacement, read one number off the vertical axis. The boat covers $45 + 70 = 115$ m and finishes at $-25$ m.

prompt: A body goes 40 m forwards along a line and then 65 m backwards. What is its displacement from the start, in metres?
explain: $40 - 65 = -25$ m. Its distance travelled is 105 m, which is a different question with a different answer.

caption: Eimear and Niall pass each other where the two lines cross.

md: Two bodies can share one set of axes, and each line is read exactly as before. The place where they cross is the moment their displacements are equal: they are at the same point on the line, passing each other. Read the time off the bottom and the position off the side.

prompt: At what time, in seconds, do Eimear and Niall pass each other?
explain: The lines cross at $(25, 200)$, so they pass after 25 s, both 200 m from the bridge.

title: You can now
md:
Read a displacement off the vertical axis, sign included.
Find a section's velocity from its own rise and its own run.
Say what a flat section and a falling section mean.
Tell a total distance apart from a final displacement.
Read where two journeys cross.

title: Sheet or memory?
md:
**On the Unit 2 formula sheet:** nothing for this topic. The sheet gives the quadratic formula, the magnitude and angle of a vector, the four constant-acceleration formulae and $F = ma$.
**Must be known:** gradient of a displacement/time graph = velocity; flat = at rest; negative displacement = the other side of the start.

prompt: Which of these is printed on the Unit 2 formula sheet?
explain: The sheet stops at the constant-acceleration formulae and $F = ma$. Everything on this page is recall.

md:
Draw a displacement-time graph from a written journey.
Read a velocity as the gradient of one section, with its sign.
Give a speed as the size of that velocity.
Use each section's own rise and run, not the clock reading.

The drawing is usually two marks: one for any two correct segments, one for the rest, so a partly right graph still scores. Mark the joints as coordinates before you rule anything. A velocity part follows, and it is read from one section's own rise and run. Stuck: draw the sections you are sure of and label the joints.
